definition: A sample of rock that contains enough of a metal-containing mineral for it to be worthwhile to extract the metal. Most metals are extracted from ores found in the Earth's crust.
msAccepts: rock containing enough metal or metal compound to make extraction worthwhile
source rock from which a metal is economically extracted
msAvoids: defining an ore as any rock containing a metal
omitting the worthwhile/economic half of the definition

definition: An individual metal compound found in rock, such as an oxide or sulfide of the metal. Minerals in real rock are mixed with unwanted material.
msAccepts: an individual compound of a metal found in the Earth's crust
e.g. iron oxides or sulfides as minerals of iron
msAvoids: using mineral and ore as identical terms — an ore is the rock, the mineral is the compound
calling native (uncombined) metals minerals

definition: Describes a metal found naturally as the uncombined element, requiring no chemical extraction. Gold is found native; silver and copper are, much more rarely.
msAccepts: exists naturally as the uncombined element
found as the element itself, not in compounds
msAvoids: saying native metals are just very pure extracted metals
attributing native occurrence to density or physical settling

definition: Heating a metal sulfide ore in air to convert it to the oxide, with sulfur dioxide released as the sulfur leaves. 2ZnS(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2ZnO(s) + 2SO₂(g).
msAccepts: heating the sulfide in air to form the oxide
sulfide + oxygen → oxide + sulfur dioxide
msAvoids: calling any heating of an ore roasting — the reactant must be a sulfide converting to oxide
omitting sulfur dioxide as the sulfur product

definition: Loss of oxygen by a substance — or, in the electron definition, gain of electrons. Obtaining a metal from its oxide is reduction of the metal compound.
msAccepts: loss of oxygen / gain of electrons
the metal oxide is reduced because oxygen is removed and the metal ion gains electrons
msAvoids: saying reduction means the substance loses electrons
naming the reducing agent as the reduced substance

definition: Gain of oxygen by a substance — or, in the electron definition, loss of electrons. At the anode in aluminium extraction, oxide ions are oxidised to oxygen.
msAccepts: gain of oxygen / loss of electrons
oxide ions losing electrons at the anode
msAvoids: saying oxidation means gaining electrons
labelling the cathode reaction as oxidation

definition: The substance that removes oxygen from another substance (donating electrons in electron terms) while being oxidised itself. Carbon reduces iron(III) oxide; carbon monoxide is the blast furnace's main reducing agent.
msAccepts: the substance taking oxygen (or donating electrons), itself oxidised
carbon (or carbon monoxide) for iron extraction
msAvoids: saying the reducing agent is reduced
naming the metal as the reducing agent in its own extraction

definition: The furnace in which iron is extracted from its ore by reduction with carbon monoxide. Detailed internal chemistry is not required by the course.
msAccepts: the tower furnace where iron ore is reduced to iron
carbon monoxide acting as the main reducing agent inside it
msAvoids: detailed furnace-stage descriptions the syllabus excludes
saying the furnace itself is the reducing agent

definition: A molten salt in which aluminium oxide is dissolved for electrolysis. It lowers the operating temperature from over 2000 °C to around 1000 °C, saving energy and money.
msAccepts: dissolves the aluminium oxide so electrolysis runs at about 1000 °C instead of over 2000 °C
its purpose is to save energy, not to react
msAvoids: calling cryolite a catalyst
saying cryolite lowers the melting point of the oxide itself rather than providing a lower-temperature medium

definition: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon. Brass (copper and zinc) and steel (iron and carbon) are standard examples.
msAccepts: a mixture of a metal with one or more elements, usually other metals or carbon
e.g. steel as iron mixed with carbon
msAvoids: calling an alloy a compound
omitting that the base must be a metal

definition: An alloy of copper and zinc. A standard named example used to test the alloy definition.
msAccepts: a mixture of copper and zinc
an alloy whose base metal is copper and whose added element is zinc
msAvoids: confusing brass with bronze (copper and tin)
giving only 'a mixture of metals' without the elements

definition: An alloy of copper and tin — among the oldest engineered alloys.
msAccepts: a mixture of copper and tin
copper hardened by the addition of tin
msAvoids: swapping the tin for zinc (that is brass)
describing bronze as a pure metal

definition: A mixture of copper and nickel, usually used to make 'silver' coins — silvery in appearance with no silver content.
msAccepts: copper and nickel alloy used for 'silver' coins
coinage metal chosen for durability and appearance
msAvoids: saying silver coins contain silver
mixing up the components with brass or bronze

definition: An alloy of iron with carbon. Many steels exist with various carbon proportions and sometimes other metals; the course limits the types to mild, high-carbon and stainless.
msAccepts: iron alloyed with carbon
alloy of iron and carbon whose properties depend on the carbon percentage
msAvoids: defining steel as a pure metal or as pure iron
forgetting that carbon, not another metal, is the defining addition

definition: Low-carbon steel, iron containing up to about 0.25% carbon. Strong, malleable and ductile; used for nails, car bodies, ships, girders and bridges; rusts and is about three times denser than aluminium.
msAccepts: iron with up to about 0.25% carbon
strong, easily shaped, used for car bodies and girders — but rusts
msAvoids: saying mild steel contains no carbon
claiming mild steel resists corrosion

definition: Steel containing about 0.6–1.2% carbon (variable), usually with small amounts of manganese. Harder and more wear-resistant than mild steel but more brittle; used for cutting tools.
msAccepts: iron with about 0.6–1.2% carbon
harder and more wear-resistant but more brittle — cutting tools
msAvoids: swapping the properties with mild steel
omitting the brittleness trade-off

definition: An alloy of iron with chromium and often nickel. Chromium forms a strong protective oxide layer, so stainless steel is very resistant to corrosion; significantly more expensive than mild steel.
msAccepts: iron with chromium (and usually nickel)
chromium's oxide layer protects the iron, giving corrosion resistance
msAvoids: attributing corrosion resistance to chromium being unreactive
omitting chromium as the anti-rust ingredient

definition: Can be easily hammered into various shapes. A property of mild steel that layers of ions sliding over each other explains — and that alloys lose when the lattice is disrupted.
msAccepts: can be hammered into shape
property explained by planes of ions sliding in the regular lattice
msAvoids: confusing malleable with ductile (drawn into wires)
explaining malleability via electrons rather than sliding ion layers

definition: Can be drawn into wires. Mild steel and copper are ductile; copper's ductility joins its conductivity to earn the electrical-wire use.
msAccepts: can be drawn out into wires
e.g. copper ductility combined with electrical conductivity for wires
msAvoids: confusing ductile with malleable (hammered into shape)
attributing ductility to strong bonding rather than sliding layers

definition: The ranked list of metals by reactivity, with carbon as the reference point that splits extraction methods: metals below it are reduced by carbon, metals above it require electrolysis.
msAccepts: metals in order of reactivity with carbon marking the carbon-reduction/electrolysis boundary
K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al above (C); Zn, Fe, Cu below (C)
msAvoids: listing metals alphabetically
omitting carbon's reference role in extraction decisions
